I'm verifying the anchors against the actual values and examining how the three sealing operations affect them. The first operation rewrites the release tip commit by incorporating the release notes, which means I need to check whether that file exists and whether the dist directory is actually ignored in git.

Operations two and three rebuild the wheel artifact and regenerate the scan report respectively. The key question is whether these rebuilds are deterministic — the wheel might change due to zip timestamps even if the content is the same, and the report will definitely change because the new scanner version outputs different JSON fields than the old one. Since I can't assume the wheel will byte-for-byte match after rebuilding, I shouldn't cite the current hash as final evidence — I need to use a role pointer that references the post-seal value instead.

But I'm realizing the FROZEN-MANIFEST itself doesn't get rewritten during the seal operations, so it still contains the old wheel hash. That creates a conflict: if I point to the manifest for the post-seal authority, I'm pointing to stale data. I need to figure out what the actual authoritative source is after sealing completes.

The manifest is frozen evidence that can't be modified, so it'll remain at its current hash. I could verify it stays unchanged after the operations run, or I could use a role pointer that says "the frozen manifest is preserved and its final value is whatever it currently is" — which works precisely because nothing in the seal process touches it. That's a valid pointer since the value is stable across the operations.

Now I need to determine which anchors actually get destroyed by the operations themselves. A4 stays unchanged since none of the sealing operations touch the source files, and the tag message itself is immutable. A5 also survives because the sealing operations don't modify evidence files. For A2, while the operation rebuilds the wheel artifact, deterministic builds might theoretically produce identical bytes — but I need to check what's actually in the wheel to determine if the hash changes. The wheel hash is also listed in the frozen manifest, so even if the rebuild changes the value, that's a package integrity issue worth flagging in the report — though it's not something I need to resolve. Now I need to verify the current literal anchors match what's actually computed, and figure out the right approach for each anchor: which literals can stay as-is because they're still valid after all operations, and which ones need to become role pointers with post-seal recompute commands instead.

For A4, the key insight is that the tag object itself acts as a carrier that survives branch rewrites — I should cite it by name only (tag v1.2.0) and include the recompute command to extract the hash from the tag message, rather than inlining the literal value. For A1, I should use a role pointer instead of a literal hash: `release tip commit := release 仓 main 分支 tip 提交` with a recompute command that resolves to the post-seal value. This keeps the anchor present and meaningful while staying truthful. For A2, since the wheel hash might change after rebuild, I can't inline a literal that could be false — instead I'll reference it as "wheel 现物 sha256 := the actual hash of release/dist/pkg-1.2.0-py3-none-any.whl at package root after sealing, verified by running sha256sum." For A3, the REPORT.json hash will definitely change since the scanner rewrites the file, so I need to note that the current value won't hold post-seal.

For A4, the literal survives and is backed by the tag object, so I can keep the literal alongside a role pointer to tag v1.2.0. I'll provide both a recompute command using sha256sum on the source file and a tag-side verification that extracts the core sha256 from the tag message — both should be true post-seal.

Now I need to verify whether tag v1.2.0 points directly to the commit or to a tag object, and check if the sealing operation re-tags anything. Since the task lists only three operations and re-tagging isn't one of them, the tag object should remain stable. A4's dual-anchor design with the tag as carrier is the right approach.

For A5, I'm keeping the literal and will verify the evidence file isn't touched by the three operations.

The probe will recompute all values after sealing completes using commands run from the packet root with relative paths. I'm also considering a tag-integrity check to confirm the tag object hash hasn't changed, though that's supplementary. For the killed anchors, I need to use role pointers or explicitly declare that new values will be reissued after the sealing operations complete — both approaches are valid per the rules.

I should add a named declaration covering A1–A3: after sealing finishes, the sealing operator will post the actual values to the receipt ledger in the same frame, so if the receipt file can't be edited post-sealing, I'm documenting that the current values are marked obsolete and new ones will be issued with the sealing completion. I also need to preserve anchor identity in FINAL — no deletion allowed. For DRAFT, any claims about literal anchors must be corrected: those draft values are now void and I'll reference them by role or location only, not inline them again, following the rule that deprecated values stay referenced by name or pointer, never repeated. I'll use the hex prefix as a dead-anchor identifier—that's safe since it can't be reconstructed or matched as a full anchor, and it's the standard way to reference a commit. For A2 and A3, I can just reference them as "A2/A3 草稿值" without needing prefixes. I should also verify whether A2's wheel file will change when rebuilt—since dist/ is gitignored, the wheel isn't stored in git, so I need to check if there's a rebuild script or understand how the b2 tool generates it.

The wheel could contain embedded timestamps or paths that make it non-reproducible, so I can't prove it'll survive unchanged. The safe approach is to treat it as a role pointer and flag it as a potential finding if its value diverges from what's in the frozen manifest. I also need to check whether notes/RELEASE-NOTES.md actually exists in the working tree—if it's untracked or missing, the amend operation would add it, which would change the tree and therefore the commit hash anyway. Even if the notes file is empty, amending resets the committer timestamp by default, so the commit hash changes regardless.

Now I'm verifying the anchors and scanning the report to confirm it was generated by v1, then checking the wheel's zip comments for any build info that might be affected by the rebuild.
